I've always had time to do every other day, but not this? That was my only, minor complaint. The part where I had to pinpoint Hancock and Juliet's positions to arrest them got me seriously scrubbing Orwell for any traces of where they had been and where they would be (It was tough, but somehow I nabbed both on the first try). The ending: oh it was more beautiful than any other game I've ever played! I had the option to incriminate Thought, or incriminate Delacroix, but I found the best solution was the most difficult. No game has ever touched me like this. Never. These developers need to get a pay raise, and I will continue buying their insanely awesome games.

After “A New Beginning” I really needed another sort of game. And “Orwell: Keeping an eye on you” is exactly that.
You start the game logging into a software system. You create a user profile. Then you watch some CCTV footage of a bomb going off in downtown Bonton (the entire game is set in a fictional world very reminiscent to our own). You’re then introduced to the database: you can create files on suspects and have to score the web to find information on them. Sometimes you encounter contrary information, and you have to decide what is true and what is false. 
This last is sometimes illogical, because the system seems to know there will be contrary information to find in the future, on pages you personally haven’t found yet. If the system already knows this, why does it need you to unlock the info in the first place? 
It’s also hard because you don’t really have any means to check the source material, and I’m as yet unaware if the storyline goes a different path if you pick another truth, or if it will self-correct and you’ll get scolded by your supervisor. Because you have an online contact who comments on everything you do, and takes further action based on the information you uncover.
Soon you also get to keep tabs on email-accounts, messaging services and phone conversations. New information will have to be checked on already visited webpages where suddenly new things are highlighted.

A really interesting mystery game where you act as a Big Brother-esque government surveillance agent thrown into an attempt to stop a series of terrorist bombings. Comb through people's computers, text messages, and phone calls, make connections, fill out their profiles, and try to discover who is responsible. 

The mystery element is really well handled. The game is challenging without feeling unfair, and I definitely liked the opportunity to have some (small) influence on the story and its conclusion. It was a lot of fun combing through the various resources to try and identify which bits and pieces of information were most important. Something unique to this game is the fact that you also have to determine how to deal with directly conflicting information and determine which information should be trusted and which shouldn't. 

Controls were all simple and intuitive. Be aware that the entire game is primarily played via interacting with text transcripts. I would almost call it something closer to interactive fiction than a more "traditional" video game, or even a visual novel. Which I love, but can understand where it may not be to some people's tastes. It's a beautifully executed idea and I had a lot of fun playing it. It is a fairly short game--maybe 7-8 hours to play through, some of which is taken up by unskippable audio conversations--but it didn't feel like it was too short or rushed.

On a more critical note, I will say that the overall "message" of the game isn't necessarily executed as well as it could be. Obviously a highly restrictive Big-Brother-esque surveillance state with, apparently, very little in the way of due process is not a good thing. But (some of) the people you are investigating have absolutely killed people and are planning to do so again. I understand that the game wants there to be tension between these ideas, but I don't know that it necessarily succeeds, especially given the fact that through careful choices on your part as an "agent" you can generally avoid any truly upsetting outcomes. It suggests more that this technology is acceptable in the "right" hands, which I'm pretty sure was not the goal of the creators. The sequel, Orwell 2, does a much better job of highlighting the ways that these types of abuses of power and surveillance can badly hurt the populace they're being used to monitor.

Orwell is a great thrilling experience. While there isn't much "Gameplay" other then reading, clicking and dragging. It still manages to pull you in with it's easily acceptable and even relevant premise, the story of The Thought group was surprisingly interesting, although it did get convoluted at the end, but it was still good. The art style is nice and the interface is super easy to use. One thing I must praise and even wanted more of had to do with this gameplay. There are some sections were reading, clicking and dragging is remixed a little. One section limits the amount of info you the database can process, and you  must genuinely think about what's most important, since before you could put in as much info as you wanted. There's another section were the entire outcome is timed, based on not only what info you gave but when and how fast it was, this was my favourite part of the game as well. It plays out a little like an escape scene, but for once your seeing all the technicalites behind it. I just wish the game tried these sections one more time as they did stand out. Another complaint is conflicting info, often you'll come across conflicting info e.g (Character was in this place at this time, character was not in place at time etc). This does make you take some decisions which did make me genuinly think and do effect the outcomes. My problem is sometimes you're forced to choose one of the two options, with only what might be coincedence to back your own point, and you can't look for some way around it. The only way to progress is sometimes by choosing something, which limits you're options and judgement on the situation. Definitly get this on sale, considering the length, but it certainly has quality! All in all, it was a great experience, great premise, thrilling sections, mostly decent choices, good artstyle and some sweet music.

Let me start with saying this: 
This game is creepy AF, if you think about it deeply. Orwell was right, even in 1948 (or 1984, depends on how you want to look at it).

Initially you're searching for details about Oleg Bakay, a missing military officer from neighboring country Parges. Soon--and for the remainder of the game--your focus shifts to Raban Vhart, a blogger whose anti-government sentiments and campaign against the leadership of The Nation (which is, yes, run by a man who looks a bit like Trump) must be thwarted. You are, essentially, the bad guy, running surveillance for a dictatorship that demands absolute fealty from the citizens it so closely monitors, but Ignorance is Strength is less explicit about the meaning behind all of this than the first game was. While Orwell stretched across five episodic instalments, Ignorance is Strength runs for just three, which winds up being too little time to build upon the previously established mythology of the game's world. The broader political climate of The Nation, the appropriately Orwellian setting for both games, isn't expanded upon much by Raban's war against it, and while a conflict with Parges is discussed it's never quite explored enough to feel like a proper plot point.

Your job is to find chunks of data online using the computer interface of the Orwell surveillance system, then throw as much dirt as you can at Raban. If a piece of information on a page can be collected, it will be highlighted, and you can drag it to their profile on your screen. You find this information by scouring websites (although annoyingly you can't "search" for sites; you either find links on sites you have already accessed or gain a new site for your database after grabbing a data chunk), and when you manage to find someone's phone or computer details you can snoop through their private screens too. Pages that haven't been fully explored, or which have data chunks you haven't lifted, are highlighted on your list of pages visited. Each piece of information you collect will eat up ten minutes on your in-game clock, and in each of the game's three episodes you're working towards a specific time limit, so you want to focus on the important information and skip over any data that does not add to the case you're building.

Sometimes data will contradict with other chunks, and as the Investigator it's up to you to choose which one to submit. The "Ethical Codex" mandate means that your supervisor is only privy to information you submit, and will make informed decisions based on that. The way the plot progresses will be influenced by which statements you decide are more valid, as you can't submit two contradictory pieces. It's an implausible system, but from a game design perspective it's a clever one, forcing you into regular moral dilemmas.

As you read through the information, the Orwell system will highlight relevant passages of text as data chunks. The system itself is incredibly literal, and unable to distinguishes nuances of language. It can't, for instance, tell that, by listing their current location as 'The Internet', your target is making a funny joke. In fact, if Orwell was analysing that last sentence, it would offer a data chunk saying I thought putting 'The Internet' as your location is a funny joke. It doesn't do sarcasm.

The obvious limitation is that you can't make recommendations. Your ability to control and shape the situation comes from the data you do or, often more crucially, don't upload. Orwell teaches this lesson early on, when a target jokes about stealing her boyfriend's credit card. Upload that data chunk and Symes, who can't see the playful dynamic of the relationship, has the card cancelled. In later episodes, the stakes are more dramatic. There are some major decisions that can have a profound effect on the story—albeit, as is often the case with episodic storytelling, the story follows the same major beats no matter your choices. But doing what seems like the noble thing doesn't always lead to the best outcome. It's complicated and messy, which feels right.

Despite these problems, Orwell is a success. It lets you watch over a spiralling conspiratorial thriller, and throws in enough twists and surprises to keep things interesting. It's an enjoyable way to interact with a world—the voyeurism creating a distinct, enjoyable power dynamic that I refuse to self-reflect on any further. It's not at all subtle—it's called Orwell, after all—but it's a well told mystery framed by a captivating storytelling device.

[quote] 𝙏𝙝𝙞𝙨 𝙘𝙤𝙢𝙢𝙚𝙣𝙩 𝙞𝙨 𝙗𝙖𝙣𝙣𝙚𝙙 𝙪𝙣𝙙𝙚𝙧 𝙍𝙪𝙡𝙚𝙨 𝙖𝙣𝙙 𝙂𝙪𝙞𝙙𝙚𝙡𝙞𝙣𝙚𝙨 𝙁𝙤𝙧 𝙎𝙩𝙚𝙖𝙢. [/quote]

This is a tricky one.

On one hand, the execution is solid. It's essentially a slightly-more-complex visual novel about parsing data from presented sources. The interface, etc, all work well for that.
(Though I do wish that linking image would be marked in some form. I spent 15 minutes trying to find a 'New Entry' on a page only to realize that a picture was actually a clickable link, in which the new entry was to be found...)

Positive shout-out to the music, too. If all you do is watch text scroll by, it's hard to build tensions... but the occasional suspense-heavy tunes that play whenever a big twist shows up on your screen, is perfectly executed.

But... then there's the actual gameplay. Which is, as said, essentially just a slightly more complex Visual Novel with some choice elements and branching paths. Which might simply not be a thing for me.

The topic portrayed in the game is very interesting, and I feel like it's handled in a perfect way. It's clear that the devs of this game want to explain the issues with an all-encompassing surveillance network to potential users, but they do so in a relatively fair and unbiased way, that (alongside countless instances of meta-commentary), essentially underline how difficult ethical use of such a system is, by inserting the player AS that ethical control mechanism. 

Lastly, I do however have to point out the longlivety and replayability of the game: 4 hours to finish, and given the core of the game is the motivation to figure out what is going on, I can't see myself playing through a second time. It's like watching a movie you already know. Nothing will surprise you, and given the only format is text, I don't think there'll be much in the ways of discovering subtle nuances and foreshadowing. There's achievements and all that for trying out different paths and endings... but I'm not going to click through a visual novel just for that.

The game comes at a low price point of 10€ though, which somewhat compensates for the point mentioned above.


In summary, I'll therefore give the 'game' a nondescript passing grade. It does not, to me, qualify as a good purchase 'for a game', but I do give it merit for being an interesting and thought-inducing piece of contemporary art.

Do not buy this if you want a lengthy, complicated mystery novel, or expect actual gameplay.

But do consider getting this if the topic of ever-increasing surveillance, and digital privacy interest you, and/or you wish to engage in an interesting 'what if' scenario.

an interesting storyline that can go in very different directions depending on your decisions. especially your decisions in the last chapter... overall fascinating to play. great design, nice unobtrusive soundtrack, realistic depictions of people and their personalities. not particularly fast-paced, but not super slow either, you can pretty much set your own pace and play as fast or slow as you want.

I love how the game has a very simple mechanic and is still so fun and entertaining. The story's great and you don't 'have' to read everything if you're annoyed by the walls of texts. But if you're like me, it gets to you and you can't help yourself but to go through it all. 
Unfortunately I played the 2nd part first so this one was much easier. Still, I probably will play again.

It is an quite interesting concept this "game" is based on. I would not describe it as a game, more like an interactive novella. It's a lot of reading and besides animations for uploads and musical support, you'll find yourself in a (partly) immersive appearing virtual working space, searching for mostly simple and flat information chains. So far, it was interesting to go through this interactive novella. Maybe it's just me, but it does not feel like if my choices really matter. Nevertheless, I enjoy the concept.

I wouldn't have thought a game consisting of mostly text and just a browser-like interface would feel like a proper videogame, but I found it a very exciting experience. At least after having figured out the ropes, which took me about half an hour. I also think the game did a great job of representing different points of view on the topic of surveillance. The only thing that irked me, however, was that your actions didn't really make a difference until the very last episode. 
9/10: would definitely [spoiler]sabotage the totalitarian government of The Nation[/spoiler]  again.

I liked it. Well written game with interesting ideas to bring to the table. Well paced, and a good length.

It's wordy by design, and has its share of flaws in terms of logic and narrative.. you need to suspend some disbelief. But it's worth it.
